lines.text: Stop adding symbols to your password if you don't want to get hacked.
Capital. Number. Symbol. This password ticks every box. And it's leaked over six million times.
Because hackers don't guess the way you think. Let's follow one password, from sign-up to cracked.
Step one. Sign-up. You type your password, and a good site does something strange. It throws it away.
First it runs it through a hash. Think of a blender. Same password in, same smoothie out. But you can't un-blend a smoothie.
So the site only keeps the smoothie. A string of scrambled characters. When you log in, it blends what you typed, and checks if they match.
Step two. The breach. One day the site gets hacked. The hackers walk out with millions of these hashes.
No passwords. Just smoothies. They can't un-blend them. So they do the next best thing. They guess.
Step three. The guessing machine. Blend a guess. Compare. Wrong? Next guess.
Sounds slow. It isn't. One gaming graphics card tries about twenty two billion guesses a second against a common fast hash.
Step four. The list. And they don't start with random letters. They start with passwords that already leaked.
One, two, three, four, five, six. Seen over two hundred million times. The word password? Fifty two million.
And here's why your symbols don't help. People add them the same way. Capital first. A one or a zero. An exclamation mark at the end.
Crackers know those tricks. They're built into the list. So that strong-looking password falls almost instantly.
So if guessing is this fast, how does any password survive?
Quick thing. Coding lessons like this, a few minutes a day, that's what you get on Teyro.
Okay. Back to the crackers.
Step five. Salt. First problem: two people with the same password get the same hash.
Crack one, you've cracked both. And hackers keep giant pre-made tables of hashes, ready to look up.
So good sites add a salt. Random text, different for every user, mixed in before blending. Same password, totally different hash.
Step six. Slow on purpose. The real problem is speed. Those common hashes were built to be fast.
So good sites use hashes that are slow on purpose, like bcrypt, or Argon two.
Same graphics card. Twenty two billion guesses a second drops to about a hundred eighty four thousand.
Now the twist. Symbols don't beat the list. Length does.
Pick four random words. From a list of seven thousand seven hundred seventy six words, that's over three quadrillion combinations.
None of them on a leak list. Against a fast hash, that's days of guessing. Against a slow one, centuries.
Even NIST, the US standards body, now tells sites: stop forcing symbols. Ask for at least fifteen characters.
One catch. Random means random. Correct horse battery staple, the famous example? Leaked over four thousand times.
To be fair, none of this helps if you reuse it. Use a different password everywhere. A password manager makes that easy.
So. Sites blend your password. Hackers steal the blends, and guess from leaked lists. Salt and slow hashes fight back. And length beats symbols.
Don't be clever. Be long.
